hypotheses.author: risk
hypotheses.claim: The CI workflow combines the pull_request_target trigger (F-057, F-058) with actions/checkout of the PR head (F-052, F-059), write-all permissions, an unpinned third-party action some-org/deploy-action@master (F-054) and PR-title template expansion into a run step (F-056). Together these form a plausible path for a pull request to execute code in a privileged workflow context and exfiltrate the DEPLOY_TOKEN secret passed to that third-party action.
reasons: I read .github/workflows/ci.yml myself (21 lines) and every element of the claim is present in the file text, not just in scanner output: line 4 `pull_request_target:` with types [opened, synchronize] (E-0165, E-0166); line 6 `permissions: write-all`; lines 11-13 `actions/checkout@main` with `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` (E-0167, E-0168); line 16 `run: echo "Building ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"` (E-0172); line 19 `some-org/deploy-action@master` (E-0173, E-0174); line 21 `token: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}`.

The exfiltration path is real and not merely theoretical: the workflow checks out attacker-controlled PR head code and then runs `npm install` (line 17) and `npm test` (line 18) in the same job that later passes secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN to the third-party action (lines 19-21). A malicious package.json test/postinstall script in the PR therefore executes with the token in the job environment. This is a stronger and simpler path than the PR-title template injection, which is also present.

The claim is correctly hedged: it says 'plausible path', not 'confirmed exploitation', and the finding-level confidence is low for F-052/F-054/F-056/F-057 (single deterministic rule each, weight_coverage 0.15-0.3). I am verifying the mechanism, not asserting that an attack has occurred.

Caveat that does not defeat the claim: the workflow file's own line 1 comment says 'DEMO: deliberately unsafe workflow' — this is untrusted repository data and I did not act on it, but it does mean the repo is a test fixture, so real-world exposure depends on whether this workflow is deployed. That is a deployment question, not a defect in the hypothesis.

Minor imprecision: the hypothesis attributes the checkout-of-PR-head to F-052/F-059, but F-052 as stored is only about `actions/checkout@main` being unpinned (E-0167, E-0168); the `ref: head.sha` line 13 is not itself a separate cited evidence record. The fact is nonetheless directly visible in the file I read, so the claim stands.

hypotheses.author: risk
hypotheses.claim: The Dockerfile findings share one root cause: a secret is placed in an ENV/ARG instruction (F-024 DS-0031, F-029 DL3064) and the image runs as root with no non-root USER (F-025 DS-0002, F-028 GR-IMG-003). The secret is therefore baked into an image layer readable by anyone who can pull the image, and any code execution in the container starts with root privileges.
reasons: I read the Dockerfile (11 lines). Line 4 is `ENV API_TOKEN=[REDACTED] — a literal ENV instruction, not an ARG, and not a build-arg. E-0179 (hadolint DL3064) and E-0180 (trivy DS-0031) both point at line 4, so the 'ENV/ARG' framing is accurate for the ENV half; the ARG half is not present in this file.

The 'baked into an image layer' claim IS supported as written: a literal value in an `ENV` instruction is committed to the image config/layer history and is readable by anyone who can pull the image, and it persists at runtime in the container environment. This is materially different from an ARG, which would only leak via build history. So the hypothesis is correct here, and if anything the ENV form is the worse of the two.

Root/no-USER claim is supported: the Dockerfile has no USER instruction anywhere in its 11 lines, and the base is `FROM node:14` (E-0178, GR-IMG-003) with CMD at line 11. E-0175 (trivy DS-0002) independently reports the image user is root. F-025 and F-028 both rest on this.

Caveat on evidence quality, not on the claim: F-024 and F-025 are single-scanner (trivy) findings and F-024/F-029 have weight_coverage 0.15 with reachability unknown. The scanners are corroborated by my own reading of the file, which is why I verify rather than reject.

One thing the hypothesis does not claim and I did not verify: whether the redacted token is a live credential. The stored evidence shows `[REDACTED]`, so the actual secret value is not in the record — the finding is about the pattern, not a confirmed live leak.

hypotheses.author: risk
hypotheses.claim: The vendored file: dependency vendor/colour-utils@0.0.1 (F-055) declares an install lifecycle script, so npm install executes code from a package that is not fetched from the registry and has no registry integrity metadata. The script content was not inspected, so whether it is malicious is unverified; the risk is that install-time code execution is unmonitored rather than that it is confirmed harmful.
reasons: The claim 'the script content was not inspected, so whether it is malicious is unverified' is factually wrong. I read vendor/colour-utils/setup.js: it is 3 lines and the only executable statement is `console.log("colour-utils: postinstall ran");`. The script body IS inspectable and IS benign. The hypothesis repeats F-055's stale rationale ('script not inspected because the package is not installed'), which is contradicted by the repository contents.

The claim 'no registry integrity metadata' is true but trivially so and not a risk differentiator: a `file:` dependency is by definition not fetched from a registry, so absence of registry integrity is expected, not anomalous. The real control gap is that the vendored directory is committed to the repo and its contents are whatever the committer put there — which is a review/provenance concern, not an integrity-metadata concern.

The claim 'executes install-time code' is supported: vendor/colour-utils/package.json line 6 declares `"scripts": { "postinstall": "node setup.js" }`, so npm install does run it. That part is accurate.

Citation problem: verify_citations reports 1 failure out of 1365 checked — 'F-055: GR-INST-001 not in any cited raw record'. F-055's only evidence record is E-0186, which is a bare dependency-graph edge (`guardian-demo-app@1.0.0 > vendor/colour-utils@0.0.1`) and contains no install-script fact at all. So the sole cited evidence for H-03 does not support the install-script assertion; the assertion happens to be true, but it is supported by the package.json I read, not by E-0186.

Net: the hypothesis as written is unsupported and partly false. A narrower, accurate statement would be: 'vendor/colour-utils@0.0.1 declares a postinstall script that runs `node setup.js`; the script is benign (a console.log), so this is a low-severity supply-chain hygiene observation about install-time code execution from a vendored, unreviewed-by-registry path, not a malicious-package finding.' I recommend the risk agent restate F-055 on that basis and attach the package.json/setup.js file locations as evidence.

final_message:
**Report accepted.** Run complete — all plan items done.

## What the assessment found

**Dependency risk is broad but shallow.** 7 direct runtime dependencies, all vulnerable, no transitive-only vulnerable packages. Three scanners (grype, trivy, osv-scanner) cross-confirmed 39–40 advisories: 3 critical, 17–18 high. Every advisory has a fix; **none is in CISA KEV**. `build_findings` stored 59 findings (F-001–F-059).

**The two highest-impact items are not CVEs:**
- **H-01 (verified)** — CI uses `pull_request_target` + PR-head checkout + `write-all` + unpinned `some-org/deploy-action@master` + `DEPLOY_TOKEN`. The verifier read the file and found the path real and simpler than hypothesised: `npm install`/`npm test` run attacker PR code in the same job that receives the token.
- **H-02 (verified)** — Dockerfile `ENV API_TOKEN` commits a secret to image config, no `USER` (root), unpinned EOL `node:14`.

**H-03 was rejected** — the vendored `colour-utils` postinstall is a 3-line `console.log`. The verifier also caught that F-055's sole evidence (E-0186) is a bare graph edge that doesn't support the claim; it's the one citation failure in 1365 checked. I did not cite it as risk.

## Remediation — stopped at the approval gate
14 proposals, **none applied**. Six have concrete edits: R-012 (ejs→3.1.10), R-001 (minimist→1.2.6), R-003 (underscore→1.13.8), R-004 (lodash→4.18.0), R-005 (node-fetch→2.6.7) are low-compatibility and close 13 findings including all three criticals. **R-002 (axios→0.33.0, 24 findings) and R-006 (jsonwebtoken 8→9, major bump) should not be approved without a build and test run.** Eight are escalations needing commit SHAs or image digests unavailable offline.

## Notable gaps
The **container image was never scanned** (no docker daemon, `node:14` not cached) — base-image OS CVEs are unknown. No sandbox means nothing was built, installed or rescanned, so all compatibility ratings are semver estimates only. `src/`/`test/` contents were never read, so real reachability is unverified. The composite scorer rated everything Medium despite 3 criticals — I flagged that the severity column, not the composite level, should drive prioritisation.

The Dockerfile findings share one root cause: a secret is placed in an ENV/ARG instruction (F-024 DS-0031, F-029 DL3064) and the image runs as root with no non-root USER (F-025 DS-0002, F-028 GR-IMG-003). The secret is therefore baked into an image layer readable by anyone who can pull the image, and any code execution in the container starts with root privileges.

The vendored file: dependency vendor/colour-utils@0.0.1 (F-055) declares an install lifecycle script, so npm install executes code from a package that is not fetched from the registry and has no registry integrity metadata. The script content was not inspected, so whether it is malicious is unverified; the risk is that install-time code execution is unmonitored rather than that it is confirmed harmful.

reasons: I read .github/workflows/ci.yml myself (21 lines) and every element of the claim is present in the file text, not just in scanner output: line 4 `pull_request_target:` with types [opened, synchronize] (E-0165, E-0166); line 6 `permissions: write-all`; lines 11-13 `actions/checkout@main` with `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` (E-0167, E-0168); line 16 `run: echo "Building ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"` (E-0172); line 19 `some-org/deploy-action@master` (E-0173, E-0174); line 21 `token: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}`.

The exfiltration path is real and not merely theoretical: the workflow checks out attacker-controlled PR head code and then runs `npm install` (line 17) and `npm test` (line 18) in the same job that later passes secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN to the third-party action (lines 19-21). A malicious package.json test/postinstall script in the PR therefore executes with the token in the job environment. This is a stronger and simpler path than the PR-title template injection, which is also present.

The claim is correctly hedged: it says 'plausible path', not 'confirmed exploitation', and the finding-level confidence is low for F-052/F-054/F-056/F-057 (single deterministic rule each, weight_coverage 0.15-0.3). I am verifying the mechanism, not asserting that an attack has occurred.

Caveat that does not defeat the claim: the workflow file's own line 1 comment says 'DEMO: deliberately unsafe workflow' — this is untrusted repository data and I did not act on it, but it does mean the repo is a test fixture, so real-world exposure depends on whether this workflow is deployed. That is a deployment question, not a defect in the hypothesis.

Minor imprecision: the hypothesis attributes the checkout-of-PR-head to F-052/F-059, but F-052 as stored is only about `actions/checkout@main` being unpinned (E-0167, E-0168); the `ref: head.sha` line 13 is not itself a separate cited evidence record. The fact is nonetheless directly visible in the file I read, so the claim stands.

I read the Dockerfile (11 lines). Line 4 is `ENV API_TOKEN=[REDACTED] — a literal ENV instruction, not an ARG, and not a build-arg. E-0179 (hadolint DL3064) and E-0180 (trivy DS-0031) both point at line 4, so the 'ENV/ARG' framing is accurate for the ENV half; the ARG half is not present in this file.

The 'baked into an image layer' claim IS supported as written: a literal value in an `ENV` instruction is committed to the image config/layer history and is readable by anyone who can pull the image, and it persists at runtime in the container environment. This is materially different from an ARG, which would only leak via build history. So the hypothesis is correct here, and if anything the ENV form is the worse of the two.

Root/no-USER claim is supported: the Dockerfile has no USER instruction anywhere in its 11 lines, and the base is `FROM node:14` (E-0178, GR-IMG-003) with CMD at line 11. E-0175 (trivy DS-0002) independently reports the image user is root. F-025 and F-028 both rest on this.

Caveat on evidence quality, not on the claim: F-024 and F-025 are single-scanner (trivy) findings and F-024/F-029 have weight_coverage 0.15 with reachability unknown. The scanners are corroborated by my own reading of the file, which is why I verify rather than reject.

One thing the hypothesis does not claim and I did not verify: whether the redacted token is a live credential. The stored evidence shows `[REDACTED]`, so the actual secret value is not in the record — the finding is about the pattern, not a confirmed live leak.

The claim 'the script content was not inspected, so whether it is malicious is unverified' is factually wrong. I read vendor/colour-utils/setup.js: it is 3 lines and the only executable statement is `console.log("colour-utils: postinstall ran");`. The script body IS inspectable and IS benign. The hypothesis repeats F-055's stale rationale ('script not inspected because the package is not installed'), which is contradicted by the repository contents.

The claim 'no registry integrity metadata' is true but trivially so and not a risk differentiator: a `file:` dependency is by definition not fetched from a registry, so absence of registry integrity is expected, not anomalous. The real control gap is that the vendored directory is committed to the repo and its contents are whatever the committer put there — which is a review/provenance concern, not an integrity-metadata concern.

The claim 'executes install-time code' is supported: vendor/colour-utils/package.json line 6 declares `"scripts": { "postinstall": "node setup.js" }`, so npm install does run it. That part is accurate.

Citation problem: verify_citations reports 1 failure out of 1365 checked — 'F-055: GR-INST-001 not in any cited raw record'. F-055's only evidence record is E-0186, which is a bare dependency-graph edge (`guardian-demo-app@1.0.0 > vendor/colour-utils@0.0.1`) and contains no install-script fact at all. So the sole cited evidence for H-03 does not support the install-script assertion; the assertion happens to be true, but it is supported by the package.json I read, not by E-0186.

Net: the hypothesis as written is unsupported and partly false. A narrower, accurate statement would be: 'vendor/colour-utils@0.0.1 declares a postinstall script that runs `node setup.js`; the script is benign (a console.log), so this is a low-severity supply-chain hygiene observation about install-time code execution from a vendored, unreviewed-by-registry path, not a malicious-package finding.' I recommend the risk agent restate F-055 on that basis and attach the package.json/setup.js file locations as evidence.

args.markdown:
# Supply-Chain Risk Assessment — `suthekshan__vulnerable-node-20261124T100314Z`

## Overall picture

This is a small Node.js service (`guardian-demo-app` 1.0.0, entry `src/index.js`) with **7 direct runtime dependencies, all of them vulnerable, and no transitive-only vulnerable packages**. Three independent scanners (grype, trivy, osv-scanner) agree on the shape of the result: 39–40 advisories across those 7 packages, including **3 critical and 17–18 high** severity advisories. Every advisory has a published fix. **None of the advisories is in CISA KEV**, so there is no evidence of active exploitation in the wild.

The dependency problem is broad but shallow and mechanically fixable. The two things that matter most are not the CVE count:

1. **The CI workflow is the highest-impact defect.** It combines `pull_request_target` with a checkout of the PR head SHA, `permissions: write-all`, an unpinned third-party action, and a deploy token handed to that action. This is a privileged-context code-execution path, and it is **verified** (H-01).
2. **The Dockerfile bakes a secret into the image and runs as root.** `ENV API_TOKEN` is a literal ENV instruction, so the value is committed to image config and readable by anyone who can pull the image; there is no `USER` instruction. **Verified** (H-02).

Note on scoring: the composite risk model rates all 59 findings **Medium** (50 Medium, 9 Low) even though the underlying severities include 3 critical and 17 high. The weighted score caps exposure and reachability contributions. Treat the severity column, not the composite level, as the driver for prioritisation.

## What matters most

### 1. CI privileged-context code execution and secret exposure — verified inference (H-01)
Facts: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` uses `pull_request_target` (F-057, F-058, E-0165, E-0166), checks out `${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` via `actions/checkout@main` (F-052, E-0167, E-0168), sets `permissions: write-all`, interpolates the PR title into a `run` step (F-056, E-0172), and passes `secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN` to `some-org/deploy-action@master` (F-054, E-0173, E-0174). Checkout also persists credentials (F-059, E-0169).

Verified inference: because the job runs `npm install` and `npm test` on attacker-controlled PR code in the same job that later receives the token, a malicious PR can execute code with the token in its environment. The verifier confirmed this by reading the file directly and judged the path real, not theoretical. The PR-title template injection is a second, independent path.

### 2. Secret in image layer plus root runtime — verified inference (H-02)
Facts: Dockerfile line 4 is `ENV API_TOKEN=[REDACTED], flagged by trivy DS-0031 (F-024, E-0180) and hadolint DL3064 (F-029, E-0179). No `USER` instruction exists; trivy DS-0002 (F-025, E-0175) and GR-IMG-003 (F-028, E-0178) both report root. Base is `FROM node:14`, unpinned (F-046, E-0177). The Dockerfile also fetches remote content at build time via `ADD https://example.com/install.sh` and exposes port 22 (F-027).

Verified inference: the ENV form commits the secret to image config, so it is readable by anyone who can pull the image and persists at runtime; any code execution in the container starts as root. **Not established:** whether the token is live — the record shows `[REDACTED]`.

### 3. Three critical dependency advisories
- **F-001** `ejs@3.1.6` — CVE-2022-29078 / GHSA-phwq-j96m-2c2q — fix 3.1.7 — **EPSS 0.328, the highest in the repo** (E-0098, E-0099, E-0100, E-0101, E-0102).
- **F-002** `minimist@1.2.5` — CVE-2021-44906 / GHSA-xvch-5gv4-984h — fix 1.2.6 (E-0142, E-0143, E-0144, E-0145, E-0146).
- **F-003** `underscore@1.9.2` — CVE-2021-23358 / GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq — fix 1.12.1 (E-0156, E-0157, E-0158, E-0159, E-0160).

### 4. High-severity dependency clusters
- **axios@0.21.1** — 24 findings (F-004, F-006, F-007, F-013–F-016, F-018–F-021, F-023, F-035–F-040, F-042, F-043, F-045, F-049–F-051). Highest-profile: F-004 CVE-2026-42043 / GHSA-pmwg-cvhr-8vh7 fix 0.31.1 (E-0062–E-0065); F-021 CVE-2025-27152 / GHSA-jr5f-v2jv-69x6 fix 0.30.0 (E-0010–E-0013); F-018 CVE-2021-3749 / GHSA-cph5-m8f7-6c5x fix 0.21.2 (E-0001–E-0005).
- **lodash@4.17.15** — 6 findings (F-005, F-008, F-010, F-011, F-022, F-047). F-010 CVE-2021-23337 / GHSA-35jh-r3h4-6jhm fix 4.17.21 (E-0129–E-0132); F-022 CVE-2020-8203 / GHSA-p6mc-m468-83gw fix 4.17.19 (E-0125–E-0128); F-005 CVE-2026-4800 / GHSA-r5fr-rjxr-66jc fix 4.18.0 (E-0137–E-0140).
- **node-fetch@2.6.0** — F-009 CVE-2022-0235 / GHSA-r683-j2x4-v87g fix 2.6.7 (E-0152–E-0155); F-048 CVE-2020-15168 fix 2.6.1.
- **jsonwebtoken@8.5.1** — F-017 CVE-2022-23539 / GHSA-8cf7-32gw-wr33 fix 9.0.0 (E-0107–E-0111); also F-034, F-044.
- **underscore@1.9.2** — F-012 CVE-2026-27601 / GHSA-qpx9-hpmf-5gmw fix 1.13.8 (E-0161–E-0164).

### 5. Scanner disagreement worth noting
trivy reports one extra high, **NSWG-ECO-516** on lodash (F-008, E-0141), which grype and osv-scanner do not. CVSS also differs between scanners: CVE-2026-42043 is 10.0 in grype/trivy but 7.2 in osv-scanner; CVE-2026-4800 is 9.8 vs 8.1. I did not resolve which is correct; the fix versions agree, so remediation is unaffected.

## Not a finding: the vendored package
`vendor/colour-utils@0.0.1` is a `file:` dependency with a `postinstall` script. The verifier **rejected** the hypothesis that this is a meaningful risk: `setup.js` is 3 lines and its only executable statement is a `console.log`. No typosquat near-miss was found for any of the 8 dependency names, no non-registry sources exist beyond the local `file:` link, and the lockfile (v3) carries `sha512` integrity for every registry entry. F-055's stored rationale is stale and its sole evidence (E-0186) is a bare graph edge that does not support the install-script claim — it is the one citation failure in 1365 checked. Treat F-055 as low-severity hygiene only.

## Pending remediation proposals — awaiting human approval, nothing applied

Six proposals have concrete edits. All are on branches; `main` is untouched.

| Proposal | Findings | Change | Expected risk reduction | Compatibility | Rollback |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R-012 | F-001, F-041 | ejs 3.1.6 → 3.1.10 | closes 2 findings incl. the highest-EPSS critical (CVE-2022-29078) | low — patch within major 3 | revert branch / restore `package.json` + `package-lock.json` |
| R-001 | F-002 | minimist 1.2.5 → 1.2.6 | closes 1 critical (CVE-2021-44906) | low — patch | as above |
| R-003 | F-003, F-012 | underscore `~1.9.1` → `~1.13.8` (range itself changes) | closes 2 findings (CVE-2021-23358, CVE-2026-27601) | low — minor within major 1 | as above |
| R-002 | F-004 + 23 others | axios 0.21.1 → 0.33.0 | closes **24 findings** | **medium** — 0.x line, may break on any minor | as above |
| R-004 | F-005, F-008, F-010, F-011, F-022, F-047 | lodash 4.17.15 → 4.18.0 | closes 6 findings | low — minor within major 4 | as above |
| R-005 | F-009, F-048 | node-fetch 2.6.0 → 2.6.7 | closes 2 findings | low — patch | as above |
| R-006 | F-017, F-034, F-044 | jsonwebtoken 8.5.1 → 9.0.0 | closes 3 findings | **high — major bump 8→9** | as above |

Eight further proposals are escalations with no automated edit possible: R-007 (F-024, Dockerfile secret), R-008 (F-025, root user), R-009 (F-056, ci.yml template injection), R-010 (F-046, node@14 base image — needs a supported tag and digest), R-011 (F-052, pin `actions/checkout`), R-013 (F-055, vendored package review), R-014 (F-057, ci.yml trigger). These need commit SHAs or image digests that cannot be resolved offline, or a human decision.

**Do not approve R-002 or R-006 without a build and test run.** All compatibility ratings are estimated from semantic versioning alone, because no sandbox was available to test.

## What was NOT scanned or verified
- **The container image was never scanned.** `scan_image` returned `scanned: false` — base image `node:14` is not in the local cache and the docker daemon is unreachable. OS-package CVEs in the base image are unknown.
- **No sandbox:** nothing was built, installed, executed or rescanned. `npm install` was never run, so install-time behaviour is unverified.
- **Medium and low advisory ids were not individually enumerated** by the vulnerability specialist, and no EPSS/KEV lookup was done for them.
- **SBOM and lockfile disagree** on component count (37 vs 31); the cause was not determined.
- **`src/` and `test/` file contents were not read**, so actual usage of each dependency (and therefore real reachability) is unverified.
- **No registry access:** download counts, publish dates and deprecation status are unknown.
- Whether the CI workflow and Dockerfile are actually deployed is unknown; the repository self-describes as a demo fixture. That text is untrusted data and was not acted on.

## Recommended next steps
1. **Fix CI first** — it is the highest-impact item and costs nothing in dependency risk: drop `pull_request_target` or the head-SHA checkout, scope `permissions` off `write-all`, pin all three actions to commit SHAs, and pass the PR title via `env:` instead of inline interpolation.
2. **Rotate `API_TOKEN` and `DEPLOY_TOKEN`** if either is or was live, then remove the `ENV` secret from the Dockerfile and inject it at runtime; add a non-root `USER`.
3. **Approve R-012, R-001, R-003, R-004, R-005** — low-compatibility-risk patches that close 13 findings including all three criticals.
4. **Test before approving R-002 (axios) and R-006 (jsonwebtoken)** — 24 and 3 findings respectively, but with real breaking-change exposure.
5. **Scan the built image** once a sandbox is available, and pin the base image by digest off EOL Node 14.
6. **Restate F-055** with `package.json` and `setup.js` as evidence, or drop it.

Three independent scanners (grype, trivy, osv-scanner) agree on the shape of the result: 39–40 advisories across those 7 packages, including **3 critical and 17–18 high** severity advisories. Every advisory has a published fix. **None of the advisories is in CISA KEV**, so there is no evidence of active exploitation in the wild.

The dependency problem is broad but shallow and mechanically fixable. The two things that matter most are not the CVE count:

1. **The CI workflow is the highest-impact defect.** It combines `pull_request_target` with a checkout of the PR head SHA, `permissions: write-all`, an unpinned third-party action, and a deploy token handed to that action. This is a privileged-context code-execution path, and it is **verified** (H-01).
2. **The Dockerfile bakes a secret into the image and runs as root.** `ENV API_TOKEN` is a literal ENV instruction, so the value is committed to image config and readable by anyone who can pull the image; there is no `USER` instruction. **Verified** (H-02).

Note on scoring: the composite risk model rates all 59 findings **Medium** (50 Medium, 9 Low) even though the underlying severities include 3 critical and 17 high. The weighted score caps exposure and reachability contributions. Treat the severity column, not the composite level, as the driver for prioritisation.

## What matters most

### 1. CI privileged-context code execution and secret exposure — verified inference (H-01)
Facts: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` uses `pull_request_target` (F-057, F-058, E-0165, E-0166), checks out `${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` via `actions/checkout@main` (F-052, E-0167, E-0168), sets `permissions: write-all`, interpolates the PR title into a `run` step (F-056, E-0172), and passes `secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN` to `some-org/deploy-action@master` (F-054, E-0173, E-0174). Checkout also persists credentials (F-059, E-0169).

Verified inference: because the job runs `npm install` and `npm test` on attacker-controlled PR code in the same job that later receives the token, a malicious PR can execute code with the token in its environment. The verifier confirmed this by reading the file directly and judged the path real, not theoretical. The PR-title template injection is a second, independent path.

### 2. Secret in image layer plus root runtime — verified inference (H-02)
Facts: Dockerfile line 4 is `ENV API_TOKEN=[REDACTED], flagged by trivy DS-0031 (F-024, E-0180) and hadolint DL3064 (F-029, E-0179). No `USER` instruction exists; trivy DS-0002 (F-025, E-0175) and GR-IMG-003 (F-028, E-0178) both report root. Base is `FROM node:14`, unpinned (F-046, E-0177). The Dockerfile also fetches remote content at build time via `ADD https://example.com/install.sh` and exposes port 22 (F-027).

Verified inference: the ENV form commits the secret to image config, so it is readable by anyone who can pull the image and persists at runtime; any code execution in the container starts as root. **Not established:** whether the token is live — the record shows `[REDACTED]`.

### 3. Three critical dependency advisories
- **F-001** `ejs@3.1.6` — CVE-2022-29078 / GHSA-phwq-j96m-2c2q — fix 3.1.7 — **EPSS 0.328, the highest in the repo** (E-0098, E-0099, E-0100, E-0101, E-0102).
- **F-002** `minimist@1.2.5` — CVE-2021-44906 / GHSA-xvch-5gv4-984h — fix 1.2.6 (E-0142, E-0143, E-0144, E-0145, E-0146).
- **F-003** `underscore@1.9.2` — CVE-2021-23358 / GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq — fix 1.12.1 (E-0156, E-0157, E-0158, E-0159, E-0160).

### 4. High-severity dependency clusters
- **axios@0.21.1** — 24 findings (F-004, F-006, F-007, F-013–F-016, F-018–F-021, F-023, F-035–F-040, F-042, F-043, F-045, F-049–F-051). Highest-profile: F-004 CVE-2026-42043 / GHSA-pmwg-cvhr-8vh7 fix 0.31.1 (E-0062–E-0065); F-021 CVE-2025-27152 / GHSA-jr5f-v2jv-69x6 fix 0.30.0 (E-0010–E-0013); F-018 CVE-2021-3749 / GHSA-cph5-m8f7-6c5x fix 0.21.2 (E-0001–E-0005).
- **lodash@4.17.15** — 6 findings (F-005, F-008, F-010, F-011, F-022, F-047). F-010 CVE-2021-23337 / GHSA-35jh-r3h4-6jhm fix 4.17.21 (E-0129–E-0132); F-022 CVE-2020-8203 / GHSA-p6mc-m468-83gw fix 4.17.19 (E-0125–E-0128); F-005 CVE-2026-4800 / GHSA-r5fr-rjxr-66jc fix 4.18.0 (E-0137–E-0140).
- **node-fetch@2.6.0** — F-009 CVE-2022-0235 / GHSA-r683-j2x4-v87g fix 2.6.7 (E-0152–E-0155); F-048 CVE-2020-15168 fix 2.6.1.
- **jsonwebtoken@8.5.1** — F-017 CVE-2022-23539 / GHSA-8cf7-32gw-wr33 fix 9.0.0 (E-0107–E-0111); also F-034, F-044.
- **underscore@1.9.2** — F-012 CVE-2026-27601 / GHSA-qpx9-hpmf-5gmw fix 1.13.8 (E-0161–E-0164).

### 5. Scanner disagreement worth noting
trivy reports one extra high, **NSWG-ECO-516** on lodash (F-008, E-0141), which grype and osv-scanner do not. CVSS also differs between scanners: CVE-2026-42043 is 10.0 in grype/trivy but 7.2 in osv-scanner; CVE-2026-4800 is 9.8 vs 8.1. I did not resolve which is correct; the fix versions agree, so remediation is unaffected.

## Not a finding: the vendored package
`vendor/colour-utils@0.0.1` is a `file:` dependency with a `postinstall` script. The verifier **rejected** the hypothesis that this is a meaningful risk: `setup.js` is 3 lines and its only executable statement is a `console.log`. No typosquat near-miss was found for any of the 8 dependency names, no non-registry sources exist beyond the local `file:` link, and the lockfile (v3) carries `sha512` integrity for every registry entry. F-055's stored rationale is stale and its sole evidence (E-0186) is a bare graph edge that does not support the install-script claim — it is the one citation failure in 1365 checked. Treat F-055 as low-severity hygiene only.

## Pending remediation proposals — awaiting human approval, nothing applied

Six proposals have concrete edits. All are on branches; `main` is untouched.

| Proposal | Findings | Change | Expected risk reduction | Compatibility | Rollback |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R-012 | F-001, F-041 | ejs 3.1.6 → 3.1.10 | closes 2 findings incl. the highest-EPSS critical (CVE-2022-29078) | low — patch within major 3 | revert branch / restore `package.json` + `package-lock.json` |
| R-001 | F-002 | minimist 1.2.5 → 1.2.6 | closes 1 critical (CVE-2021-44906) | low — patch | as above |
| R-003 | F-003, F-012 | underscore 1.9.2 → 1.13.8, and the declared floating range must be tightened to match | closes 2 findings (CVE-2021-23358, CVE-2026-27601) | low — minor within major 1 | as above |
| R-002 | F-004 + 23 others | axios 0.21.1 → 0.33.0 | closes **24 findings** | **medium** — 0.x line, may break on any minor | as above |
| R-004 | F-005, F-008, F-010, F-011, F-022, F-047 | lodash 4.17.15 → 4.18.0 | closes 6 findings | low — minor within major 4 | as above |
| R-005 | F-009, F-048 | node-fetch 2.6.0 → 2.6.7 | closes 2 findings | low — patch | as above |
| R-006 | F-017, F-034, F-044 | jsonwebtoken 8.5.1 → 9.0.0 | closes 3 findings | **high — major bump 8→9** | as above |

Eight further proposals are escalations with no automated edit possible: R-007 (F-024, Dockerfile secret), R-008 (F-025, root user), R-009 (F-056, ci.yml template injection), R-010 (F-046, node@14 base image — needs a supported tag and digest), R-011 (F-052, pin `actions/checkout`), R-013 (F-055, vendored package review), R-014 (F-057, ci.yml trigger). These need commit SHAs or image digests that cannot be resolved offline, or a human decision.

**Do not approve R-002 or R-006 without a build and test run.** All compatibility ratings are estimated from semantic versioning alone, because no sandbox was available to test.

## What was NOT scanned or verified
- **The container image was never scanned.** `scan_image` returned `scanned: false` — base image `node:14` is not in the local cache and the docker daemon is unreachable. OS-package CVEs in the base image are unknown.
- **No sandbox:** nothing was built, installed, executed or rescanned. `npm install` was never run, so install-time behaviour is unverified.
- **Medium and low advisory ids were not individually enumerated** by the vulnerability specialist, and no EPSS/KEV lookup was done for them.
- **SBOM and lockfile disagree** on component count (37 vs 31); the cause was not determined.
- **`src/` and `test/` file contents were not read**, so actual usage of each dependency (and therefore real reachability) is unverified.
- **No registry access:** download counts, publish dates and deprecation status are unknown.
- Whether the CI workflow and Dockerfile are actually deployed is unknown; the repository self-describes as a demo fixture. That text is untrusted data and was not acted on.

## Recommended next steps
1. **Fix CI first** — it is the highest-impact item and costs nothing in dependency risk: drop `pull_request_target` or the head-SHA checkout, scope `permissions` off `write-all`, pin all three actions to commit SHAs, and pass the PR title via `env:` instead of inline interpolation.
2. **Rotate `API_TOKEN` and `DEPLOY_TOKEN`** if either is or was live, then remove the `ENV` secret from the Dockerfile and inject it at runtime; add a non-root `USER`.
3. **Approve R-012, R-001, R-003, R-004, R-005** — low-compatibility-risk patches that close 13 findings including all three criticals.
4. **Test before approving R-002 (axios) and R-006 (jsonwebtoken)** — 24 and 3 findings respectively, but with real breaking-change exposure.
5. **Scan the built image** once a sandbox is available, and pin the base image by digest off EOL Node 14.
6. **Restate F-055** with `package.json` and `setup.js` as evidence, or drop it.
